extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, sociology students, and researchers studying press representations of crime and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and conventions newspapers use when constructing and resolving news about crime (headlines, sources, framings, transitions to editorials/features, typographical treatment, ideological closure). Useful for media analysis and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credence to actors with personal involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Give particular credibility to actors who have personal and intimate involvement in the event (victims, victims' families, accused's relatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quoting the victim or mothers as 'the human face of the drama' and using personal comments to personalise accused (e.g. 'a good boy', 'very shocked'). This anchors the abstract stereotype of criminality in a real person and environment and tends to evoke sympathy or tacit approval of punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing the event as having wider political/judicial implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the event as marking a development in an ongoing public/judicial debate by situating it within wider institutional discourse (interest groups, pressure groups, elected representatives, academic experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting bodies like PROP, the Howard League, Police Federation or ministers moves the story from isolated incident to part of a larger politicised 'law-and-order' issue, enabling editorial/political closure beyond the courtroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard story pattern (headline, photo, court account, institutional quotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct primary-news items with a common set of elements: an attention-grabbing headline (often age/sentence juxtaposition), photographs, an account of court proceedings, statements from the affected individuals, and comments from institutionalised spokesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this as the 'pattern common to most of the newspapers' and implies that presence/absence or emphasis of these elements shapes the story's angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of politico-juridical quotations to politicise judicial outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote speeches and statements from ministers and senior officials to imply that sentences align with government thinking, thereby breaching the conventional separation of judiciary and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Times and Guardian quoting Lord Colville, the Home Secretary, and Lord Hailsham. Effect: the sentence is moved to a political level and linked to a broader mugging campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical tactics to legitimate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce crime statistics (e.g., '129 per cent rise in muggings') to imply objective justification for drastic sentences and to close debate by appealing to 'hard evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by papers like The Times and Telegraph to support the necessity of punitive measures; acts as a 'closure' device by suggesting an unprecedented crime wave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal 'objective' style that is legally inflected
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an ostensibly objective, balanced report that nonetheless is framed by legalistic/institutional perspectives (e.g., quoting police chiefs, capsule judge biographies) which tilt the piece toward the 'judicial' camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although quotes from penal reformers are included, the strategic use of primary definers (police statements, judge background) can outweigh humane/personalised elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalised, dramatised tabloid treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the event in a popular-demotic style: dramatise, personalise, and cast differing views in moral 'common-sense' terms rather than legalistic ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirror example: stretched headline emphasizing 20 years then age; strict typographic balance of opposing moral views; absence of crime statistics; reliance on parents' testimony to humanise accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical layout as a signalling device for balance/controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use layout (juxtaposed columns, headlines, supporting headlines) to literalise balance and indicate controversy, inviting readers to adjudicate between presented sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mirror's two-column juxtaposition with contrasting column headlines presenting opposing moral frames: one personalised, one emphasising gangs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the story as a quasi-argument (polarised two-sided frame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orchestrate the news item as a debate between two poles (e.g., age of offenders vs length of sentence), elaborating and contrasting both sides via quotations and structural emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces news value through polarity; primary-news treatment casts the report 'in the form of a question' or issue to be resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal balance can mask partisan inflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where formal balance exists, selection, personality and habitual angling of a paper may inflect that balance to favour one perspective (legalistic/institutional vs humane/personalised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The personality of the paper or how subjects are normally angled (see earlier chapters) often determines which side 'commands the field' despite apparent balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from primary news to editorials/features as modes of closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from initial event-reporting (foreground) to editorials (judgement) or features (background/explanation) to provide different kinds of 'answers' and ideological closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials tend toward a judgemental closure; features pursue deeper explanations and background. The interplay is both formal and ideological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials as instruments of ideological closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use editorials to effect a relatively simple ideological closure—often aligning with conventional viewpoints (e.g., support for sentences)—thereby marginalising alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Handsworth case most editorials supported the sentences; editorials generalise from the event to abstract societal concerns and justify law's firmness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required to sustain pro-punitive argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Pro-sentence editorial arguments depend on acceptance of three propositions: that violent crime is spiralling; that there is a distinct 'mugging' phenomenon; and that public protection outweighs offender reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter stresses these as necessary assumptions for the dominant editorial line; if any are challenged the argument weakens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction of 'society' and perception of law as autonomous
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'society' as an abstract collective interest and portray the law as an autonomous institution acting for that abstract public, which facilitates morally totalising editorial arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves excluding particular groups' perceptions and dissolving concrete social experience into a generic 'public' that the law supposedly protects.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-dimensional language and labelling precludes analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a tight set of labels and clichéd language (e.g., 'mugger', 'for kicks', 'violent playground') that absorb conceptual content into standardized words, preventing nuanced analysis or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sun is cited as exemplary: exclusive victim focus and label-driven reporting make features and editorials superfluous and preclude debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature conventions: seeking background elements
rubrics_metrics.description: In feature work journalists look for 'background' elements—people, places, experiences, local opinion, councillors, social workers, academic reports—and explore these to contextualise the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features weigh these elements against each other and may use typographical formats to balance perspectives; they draw on a wider ideological field than primary news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature dynamics: contextualisation and ideological reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Features extend the problem from immediate strategy to causes and motivations, using established journalistic conventions to identify patterns (what kinds of youths, backgrounds, area characteristics) and relate them to social problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This movement depends on cues from the initial news thematisation and is conceptually distinct from primary-news values, often opening up alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of primary definers and capsule biographies to direct interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ statements from authoritative figures (primary definers like police assistant commissioners) and brief biographical details (of judges, offenders) to steer readers toward a particular interpretive frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Assistant Commissioner Woods' statement framing mugging as symptom of violent society or capsule biography highlighting judge's prior remarks—both serve to legitimate the judicial perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of personal viewpoint columnists as institutionalised dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow regular columnists to offer provocative dissenting takes outside the formal news/editorial structure, but confine them institutionally so their effect remains limited by the dominant news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Akass and Waterhouse provided radical voices, but their institutional position meant their dissent was token relative to massive coverage dominated by conventional values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of exploration (features) from advocacy (editorials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain functional distinctions: features are committed to investigation and 'getting inside' background complexities, while editorials pursue advocacy and judgement; both derive from primary-news themes but answer differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasises that the separation is not merely technical but reflects two different ways of producing ideological closure—simple (editorial) vs complex (feature).
